rowGroups: The <IDS definition group> is the default decomposition; the <IDS alternative group> splits the character into less reasonable, uncommon components.
rowYan: Normally split as ⿰氵艳, not as the alternative ⿰沣色.
rowVariants: The IDS of the variants are separated by ;, and each variant is followed by its glyph variant identifier in parentheses ().
u31ef: Note: U+31EF is special because it is not in the Ideographic Description Characters block, probably because that block has no room left.
tagAfter: A region identifier after a character means the character takes that region's glyph.
tagEnd: A region identifier in parentheses at the end of an IDS means the IDS applies to that region's glyph.
tagOmit: Note: a character with no glyph variants may leave out the identifier.
sourceG: Mainland China (only for a 彐 (U+5F50) that does not match the abstract shape)
sourceQ: UTN #53, the UCS2003 column before Unicode 13.0; CJK Unified Ideographs Extension B only
sourceAny: Every source that matches the abstract shape; G by default (except the case above)
precedence: When the IDS of several sources' glyphs are the same, the source identifier that comes first in the Unicode code chart stands for them.
ucv: The identifier then starts with q (or p for 撇, x for crossing, y for other), followed by the UCV rule's three-digit number (padded with 0), then the index of a glyph within that rule (one digit from 1 if the rule has fewer than 10 variants, else two digits from 01), and may end with a lowercase x or y for other variants.
imaginary: When a new variant is made by analogy from a component of one or more UCV rules, the identifier starts with qq, followed by one or more three-digit UCV rule numbers (padded with 0).
zhi: No IDS of 卮 includes this UCV, so qq123 switches the 㔾 in 卮 to this form (巳).
alternate: When a character has variants that differ at the stroke level or in the position of some components, the identifier is written with lowercase letters, dots and digits.
compose: The full identifier joins, in component order, each component's stroke-style character or the identifier it uses.
feng: The first two parts of 丰 are unchanged; in the third part, a stroke resembling 撇 becomes 撇.
xun: A part of 勳 (灬) moves a little to the right.
zi: Although the middle of 子t (the left of 孩) looks like a 提 #(T), it is 一t, a 一 bent to make room.
mirror: A mirrored character, or a variant with a mirrored component.
similar: The character this IDS forms resembles the original (?), but no UCV rule covers it.
otherKinds: Identifiers starting with j, q or a digit mark other kinds of stroke difference, e.g. (jss), (qy), (2t)…
custom: Any identifier that follows the EBNF above and clearly tells apart the IDS of a character's glyph variants is a valid identifier.
chainWhy: Some characters contain structures that plain IDS describes poorly, or only by referring to themselves, such as 乙, 亞, 凸, 一…
chain: The strokes of a chain join end to start in order and are written in one continuous line, hence the name. Writing angles are ignored; only each stroke's start, end and change of thickness count. A chain is one unit: when it crosses or overlaps other components, its stroke order and joins stay as written.
clockwise: Note: Q (circle) curves are written clockwise.
modW: Only after SH or PH: the joint where the horizontal starts is rounder, as in ㇄ #(SHw). Not to be confused with the stroke W.
modG: The stroke ends in a hook, as in ㇁ #(Wg). Only after H, S, P, N and W; with w it comes after w, as in ㇈ #(HSHwg).
reverse: Before a stroke: the stroke is joined in reverse, its start and end swapped.
cross: After a stroke, followed by a positive integer n: the stroke crosses the n-th stroke of its chain, counting from 0.
break: After a stroke: a forced break. Normalization may not join it with the next stroke into another stroke, but the next stroke still starts where this one ends.
nian: The 凵 of 廿 is written as three strokes.
ao: Without b it would normalize to #(一-𠃍𠃊-𠃍𠃊).
closed: At the end of a chain: the chain closes on itself.
curveStart: Start of a curve: an open curve starts at its clockwise end; a closed curve starts at its lowest-left segment.
curveReverse: The connector applies to curves too.
oldLetters: B flat, D dot, G hook, H horizontal, N right-falling, P left-falling, Q circle, S vertical, T rising, W bend, X slant, Z turn (case-insensitive).
oldConnector: The connector is a minus sign -; a stroke preceded by it is written backwards.
firstLetters: H is horizontal, S vertical, P left-falling, w bend, g hook.
firstJoins: Put a connector between each pair of characters and draw the shape in order: > joins end to start, ^ start to start, v end to end.
firstCurves: When curves cross, number each curve from 0 and add the codes of the crossing pairs at the end of the curve IDS.
roles: In ⿻字₁字₂, 字₁ is the vertical component and 字₂ the horizontal one.
forms: The overlap extension has two versions, quick and full, plus one special case.
slice: A positive integer before, a (usually negative) integer after, separated by a colon. Either may be left out, not both. Horizontals are numbered from 0, top down; negatives count from the bottom, and -1 is the last horizontal.
sliceTouch: ⿻[a:b]字₁字₂ (a, b positive) means the tops of all verticals in 字₁ touch just below the a-th horizontal of 字₂ (as in 丅), and their bottoms touch just above its b-th horizontal (as in 丄).
virtual: Horizontal 0 (a virtual line above the first) or horizontal -0 (a virtual line below the last).
sign: Before the colon, prefer a positive a, unless counting back gives a smaller x in -x (such as -1); after the colon, prefer a negative -y, unless the positive b is smaller than y (such as 1).
you: ⿻[:-1]丨日 stands only for 由, never for 甲, 申, 甴 or 曱.
cellSegments: If the vertical has several segments, mark them a, b, c… from top to bottom.
cellDot: Otherwise, if vertical j of 字₁ ends against horizontal i of 字₂ (as in 丅 or 丄, touching or not), the cell is .
cellUnder: Otherwise, if horizontal i of 字₂ ends against vertical j of 字₁ (as in ⺊ or ┤, touching or not), the cell is _
segmentDefault: ⿻[a]字₁字₂, like ⿻[x]字₁字₂, is the default and takes no crossing expression; ⿻[a]㇉一 is written ⿻㇉一.
qu: Left unsimplified, it would wrongly be written [,,.].
yin: ㇋ has two vertical segments (a vertical and a 撇); 乀 crosses segment b, the 撇.
zhao: 弓z (its last stroke is ㇥) has three vertical segments (the vertical of 𠃍, the vertical of ㇥, the 撇 of ㇥); 丶 crosses segment c, the 撇.
shen: 冂 has a vertical and a vertical hook; 丿 passes under the vertical (.), then crosses the vertical hook (x).
tiShape: 〢 crosses the first horizontal (an empty row); the first vertical of 〢 meets the rising stroke below (., as in 丄), and that stroke meets the second vertical from the left (_, as in ┤).
hookT: 𦉫T has a hook at the bottom right.
reverseMatrix: [fr,on,t|ba,ck], where the bar | separates the forward matrix from the reverse one.
curveCase: So the brackets here do not give crossings; they only say whether each Q part of the curve lies left (l) or right (r) of the vertical component. This is the only character known to need it.
oldMarks: ⿻[s]字¹字²: s is a superimpose mark. When 字² has more than one stroke, write ⿻[s,s,s…]字¹字² with (strokes of 字² − 1) commas; the n-th s applies to the n-th stroke of 字².
index: x is a positive integer: 字₂ goes into the (x + 1)-th fully enclosed space of 字₁ (日 here), counted top to bottom, middle first, then left to right. When x is 0 (the first space), [0] is left out.
indexHalf: In ⿵⺵丶 the half-enclosure is ⿵, enclosing from above, left and right (like 冂), so ⺵ has three ⿵ spaces: from left to right [0] (left out by default), [1] and [2].
indexYi: 㠯 has two fully enclosed spaces: the inner IDS puts 一 in the upper one, and the outer [1] puts 一 in the lower one.
subtract: ㇯字₁字₂ is what remains of 字₁ once 字₂ is taken out. Since 字₁ may hold several 字₂, brackets after ㇯ say which one goes, counted left to right, top to bottom, from 0. [0], the first, may be left out.
subtractSearch: Subtraction is not used in the IDS database; it is only for quick searches on zi.tools.
subtractChain: Parts of 字₁ made of a stroke chain cannot be counted or removed. ㇯[1]日一 is invalid: the frame of 日 is 口, a chain (#(-丨𠃍-一z)), so its horizontal cannot be removed; ㇯日一 gives 口.
sub0: 王 without its 0th 一, the top one
unique: So that every IDS maps back to exactly one character, a unique separator naming the abstract shape goes before the IDS.
uniqueRare: The separator goes on the rarer character, not the more common one.
uniqueStroke: Characters whose stroke chain equals one in the CJK Strokes block get a separator.
uniqueQuestion: An IDS that differs much from the character's other sources and collides with another code point also gets one: a question mark (and one digit?) goes before the character, as {?字} or {?0字}.
uniqueSource: An IDS for a particular source may add that source's identifier after the character: {字T} is the T source.
yue: {曰}⿴囗一 stands only for 曰, never for 日.
oral: No public material covers this part yet; it comes only from Yi Bai's oral explanation.
abstract: The abstract shape: a character may take different variant components and still be recognized and told apart by its meaning.
dedupe: The braces hold the abstract shape, there only to remove duplicates; otherwise two IDs would share one IDS.
replace: 🔄︎字₁字₂字₃ is 字₁ with its component 字₂ replaced by 字₃. It is mainly for quick searches on zi.tools and is not used in the zi.tools IDS database.
lv2: ids_lv2.txt: components merged by the Unicode UCV list
lv1Merge: In ids_lv1 (the one zi.tools uses) every stroke-level difference, such as 丶 and 乀 in the same place, is merged.
lv2Merge: Components are replaced, where possible, by their forms in common G-source characters; components the UCV list calls "must unify" are merged too.
ebnf: Compiled by @NightFurySL2001 for reference only; not a formal definition.
stroke.Z: leftward (only in ㇘ #(SZ), for the Kangxi Dictionary form)
stroke.Wg: bending hook (W never stands alone; it is always Wg)
